pathwayLabel: Certification by Endorsement — 10-Year Licensure History (Option C) — Reciprocity Not Available for This Classification
steps: Florida's Reciprocity form (DBPR CILB 32, restricted to Louisiana) does not offer Class A or Class B Air-Conditioning as a license category at all — confirmed directly from the form's own category checklist. Reciprocity is not available to HVAC contractors in Florida regardless of home state.
The applicable route instead is DBPR CILB 10, Certification by Endorsement (Section 489.115(3), Florida Statutes), which does list Class A and Class B Air-Conditioning as selectable categories.

Within CILB 10, the NASCLA-based Option A does not apply to this classification — the form explicitly restricts it to 'General, Building, and Residential license' only. The applicable route for a California C-20 contractor is Option C: hold a valid, current out-of-state license for at least 10 years, active now or within the last 2 years.

needs_review: CILB 10's 2-hour Florida Building Code course requirement is explicitly scoped in the document to General, Building, Residential, and Roofing Contractor applicants only — Class A/B Air-Conditioning is not listed. Whether AC applicants face this same requirement, a different one, or none at all is not stated in the document and is not assumed here either way.
Submit electronic fingerprints, a FICO-derived credit report, and proof of satisfaction of any liens, judgments, or bankruptcy.
Pay the $354 Endorsement application fee to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
Await processing — DBPR does not publish a guaranteed timeline; budget for several weeks to a few months.
notes: Confirmed directly from DBPR CILB 32 (Reciprocity) and CILB 10 (Endorsement), the same documents sourced for the florida-california contractor pair, re-read specifically for HVAC scope. CILB 32's own category checklist offers only General/Building/Residential Contractor for its one reciprocal state (Louisiana) — no Air-Conditioning option exists on that form at all, so Reciprocity is structurally unavailable to HVAC contractors in Florida, not just unavailable to California specifically. CILB 10 does list Class A and Class B Air-Conditioning as selectable categories, and its $354 fee is not category-specific (same figure confirmed for the contractor pair). needs_review: whether the 2-hour Florida Building Code course applies to Class A/B AC applicants is genuinely unconfirmed — the document scopes that specific requirement to General/Building/Residential/Roofing only, and does not state what (if anything) applies to Air-Conditioning applicants instead. Left as an open question rather than assumed in either direction. CORRECTION (2026-09-20): this record originally stated CILB 32's reciprocal-state list as 'Louisiana, Mississippi, and North Carolina.' That was wrong. Re-verified by running antiword directly on the raw CILB 32 .doc binary (bypassing both flrules.org's Cloudflare bot-challenge, which blocks plain curl, and any AI-summarization step) — a full-text search of the complete extracted document found 'Louisiana' three times, in the three license-category checkboxes, and zero occurrences of 'Mississippi' or 'North Carolina' anywhere. The form's instructions do reference an external hyperlink whose destination this extraction can't follow, so a broader, separately-maintained list is conceivable — but the form's own selectable categories name only Louisiana. This record's conclusion (California doesn't qualify for reciprocity either way, and no A/C category exists on CILB 32 regardless) is unaffected by the correction.
officialSourceName: Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation, Construction Industry Licensing Board (DBPR CILB)
